abcc590750:
This chapter is a first-principles look at the one endpoint every Claude application calls: POST /v1/messages. It covers:

  • the request and response shapes, the two roles and the system prompt;
  • typed content blocks and the usage record;
  • every documented stop_reason;
  • why the API is stateless, and what that forces your code to do;
  • prefill, and why newer models reject it;
  • the tool and thinking parameters as they appear on the wire;
  • every documented error status, retries and rate limits;
  • the Python and Java SDKs.

The story runs from the Text Completions API and its Human:/Assistant: prompt format to today's typed block protocol.
a4466f5e12: Neighbouring chapters: chapter 06 covers streaming, vision, PDFs, the Files API, citations, data-access patterns and Bedrock/Vertex. Chapter 07 covers the Batch API. Chapter 13 covers sampling, thinking and effort as concepts. Chapter 14 covers the raw HTTP and server-sent-event layer under the SDKs, chapter 15 caching and cost, and chapter 21 tool implementation. This chapter owns the shape of one request and one response, and everything that can go wrong between them.
ec946cd186:
The Messages API is one stateless function: you send the model ID, an output cap, an optional system prompt and the entire conversation as a list of typed content blocks, and you get back exactly one assistant turn plus a stop_reason that tells your code what to do next.

Everything that makes an integration reliable lives in your code, not on the server: keeping and resending the transcript, branching on stop_reason rather than on the text, answering every tool call in the next turn, and classifying errors so you retry only what a retry can fix.
37f52a961d:
Those two sentences cover most of what objective 2.3 asks at the mechanics level. The rest of the chapter unpacks them:

  • what each request field does, and why it's there;
  • why the response is a list of blocks and not a string;
  • the seven stop reasons, and the handler each one needs;
  • what statelessness costs you, and what it buys;
  • why prefill used to be a format trick and is now a 400 on the newest models;
  • the error, retry and rate-limit behaviour that decides whether your service survives its first busy Monday.
4282bf16a5:
The CCDV-F guide lists objective 2.3 as "messages, tools, streaming, vision, thinking, caching, third-party vendors (Bedrock/Vertex), Messages API data access patterns, Batch API, realtime vs batch tradeoffs". At 6.8% of 53 items, that's three or four questions. But mechanics also appear inside questions on debugging (D4), cost (5.4) and output handling (6.3).

The stems are recognisable: "the integration intermittently returns half a JSON object", "the chatbot forgets the customer's name", "retries make the outage worse", "the request fails with 400 after the model calls two tools". Each has one mechanical cause. The distractors are usually model-quality fixes (a bigger model, a better prompt) for what is really a protocol bug.
cbe62664e0: The Messages API looks obvious today. But each of its design choices replaced something that caused real bugs. Knowing what came before explains why the current rules exist. And several exam distractors are leftovers from earlier designs.
18dfe26592:
Early language-model APIs, including Anthropic's original Text Completions endpoint (/v1/complete), took a single prompt string and returned a continuation. A conversation was just a convention inside that string. Anthropic's format alternated Human: and Assistant: markers. The prompt had to end with Assistant: so the model knew whose turn it was.

The model was a next-token predictor, and the API exposed that directly. You wrote the start of a document, and it wrote the rest.
c1aa13abe2:
That design had three problems, and the Messages API was built to remove them.

First, structure was in-band. Turn boundaries were just characters. A user who typed \n\nHuman: into a chat box could forge a turn. It's the same class of bug as SQL injection, where data is parsed as control.

Second, everything was text. There was no way to send an image, a document or a structured tool call except by encoding it into the string. Then you parsed the answer back out with regular expressions.

Third, the stop signal was weak. You learned that the model stopped. But telling "finished" from "cut off" from "wants to call a function you described in prose" was your problem.
ebf41628ab:
The industry's answer, popularised by chat-completion APIs in 2023, was to send a list of messages, each with a role and content. Turn boundaries moved from characters into the JSON structure, so a user can't forge a turn by typing a marker.

Anthropic's Messages API (generally available in early 2024; check the docs for the exact date) followed the same idea, with two deliberate differences that the exam likes to probe. The system prompt is a top-level field, not a message with role: "system". And content is a list of typed blocks from day one, not a string that later grew attachments. The anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 header that you still send on every request pins that wire contract.
ef6bca359c:
Once content was a typed list, new capabilities became new block types rather than new endpoints:

  • Tool use (generally available in 2024) added tool_use blocks in assistant turns and tool_result blocks in user turns, with ids that tie them together, plus the tool_use stop reason.
  • Images and PDFs became image and document blocks.
  • Extended thinking (2025) added thinking and redacted_thinking blocks carrying an opaque signature.
  • Server-side tools such as web search added their own block types and the pause_turn stop reason.

The request and response envelope barely changed while the capability surface grew. That's exactly what a polymorphic message format is for.
9f62c6d4c1:
The most recent changes all run in one direction. Features that let the client steer the raw token stream are being replaced by declared intent.

  • Assistant prefill (writing the first tokens of the model's answer) is rejected with a 400 on Claude 4.6 and later models. Structured outputs and strict tool schemas replace it.
  • Manual thinking budgets (budget_tokens) give way to adaptive thinking with an effort level.
  • On the newest models, non-default temperature, top_p and top_k are rejected outright.

And a new escape hatch arrived in the other direction. On the newest models, a role: "system" message may appear after a user turn. It adds instructions mid-conversation without invalidating the cached prefix.

Each of these is a breaking change for code written a year earlier. That's why objective 5.3 lists "breaking changes across releases", and why section 10 and section 12 spend time on them.
17a17bd0d7: Distractors often describe a technique that was correct for an older model or API: "prefill an opening brace to guarantee JSON", "put the instructions in a system-role message at the start of the messages array", "lower the temperature to 0 for deterministic output". Each was reasonable once. On the current models named in the guide, each one either fails with a 400 or isn't the best answer. When an option sounds like a trick from 2023, check it against the current rules.
477f2b5ae7:
Strip the API down and it is one function: f(model, system, messages, tools, settings) → next assistant turn. You send the entire conversation so far. The model reads all of it as one token sequence. It generates the next assistant message token by token until one of five things happens: it decides it has finished, it hits your max_tokens cap, it emits one of your stop sequences, it fills its context window, or it asks to call a tool.

The server returns that one message and keeps nothing. There is no session id, no server-side conversation object and no "continue" endpoint. The docs say it plainly: the Messages API is stateless, so you always send the full conversational history.
e9a02e6fb8:
Why build it this way? For the same reasons you made your Spring microservices stateless.

A stateless endpoint scales horizontally. Any replica can serve any request, because the request carries everything. So the provider can route each call to whichever GPU node has capacity, with no sticky sessions or shared session stores.

Failure is simpler too. If a replica dies mid-request, nothing is lost except that request. A retry carries the same full context to another replica.
890ed29734:
For you, the more important consequence is that the client owns the context. Before every call, your code decides what the model will see: which turns to keep, which tool outputs to trim, which facts to pin at the top, what to redact. That's what makes context engineering (chapter 03 and objective 6.1) possible at all. A stateful server would have to make those choices for you, with a policy you couldn't inspect.

It also means earlier turns don't have to come from Claude. You can write synthetic assistant turns, such as few-shot examples as a fake conversation, or a summary standing in for twenty real turns. The model treats them as history.
a658c73579:
The cost is real, and it grows with every turn. You pay input tokens for the whole history on every call, and latency grows with input length. A forty-turn support chat resends turn one forty times.

Prompt caching (chapter 15) exists largely to soften this. A stable prefix written to the cache once is read back cheaply on later calls. Section 09 works through the numbers.
88068e7ccc: The Java analogy is a REST service that uses a self-contained JWT instead of an HttpSession. The token travels with every request. If the client drops a claim, the server never knew it. Likewise, if your code drops turn 3 from the array, the model never saw turn 3. Most "the bot forgot what I said" bugs are exactly that.
eb53420a10: Here is a complete request as it goes over the wire. The SDKs build exactly this, so it's worth reading once in raw form. Chapter 14 goes further into the HTTP layer.
49e9f739d4:
Three headers matter.

  • x-api-key authenticates the call against a workspace in your organisation.
  • anthropic-version pins the API contract, meaning the request and response wire format. It is entirely separate from the model version: the same 2023-06-01 header works with every current model.
  • anthropic-beta, when present, opts in to a named beta feature. Its values are dated strings such as model-context-window-exceeded-2025-08-26.

The SDKs set the first two for you from the environment, and let you pass betas per call.
ab29e40453:
Notice what is not in the request: temperature. On the newest models (the docs list Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and other recent releases), any non-default temperature, top_p or top_k returns a 400 on every request, whether or not thinking is on. Older models such as Haiku 4.5 still accept them.

So if your configuration management (chapter 10) sets temperature: 0 globally, upgrading the model ID breaks every call. Example 10_thinking_params.py shows the failure.
90a9830233:
Inside messages there are two everyday roles: user and assistant. The conversation must start with a user turn. A request whose first message is anything else is rejected.

Assistant turns are whatever the model said before, or whatever you choose to say it said. User turns are not only what the human typed. Tool results travel in user turns too, because from the model's point of view they are input from the outside world.
11829d6eb9:
The system prompt is a separate top-level system field. It's where durable instructions belong: the role, rules, output format, the policy document, the tone. The user turn carries the task and the data.

This split isn't cosmetic. The model is trained to give the system prompt more authority than user content, so the placement is part of your security design (chapter 19 and objective 7.1). Content you didn't write, such as a web page, an email body or a customer's free text, belongs in a user turn inside clear delimiters. Never concatenate it into the system prompt, where it would inherit that authority.
9e1cd3d80a:
The most common mistake carried over from other vendors' chat APIs is to put {"role": "system", ...} as the first element of messages. On the Messages API that's a 400. A system message can never be the first entry.

The newest models do accept a role: "system" message after a user turn. (The docs list Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and several other recent models; check the docs for your model.) It adds instructions partway through a conversation, for example "the customer has now passed identity verification; account tools are allowed". Such a message has the same authority as the top-level field. And because it's appended at the end of the history, it doesn't invalidate a cached prefix.

On models that don't support it, the same message is a 400. Example 02_roles_and_order.py runs all five cases.
b2525a4d46:
What about two user turns in a row, or two assistant turns? The working-with-messages guide doesn't spell out a rule, and you shouldn't depend on whatever the API does with them. Write your code to alternate cleanly: merge consecutive user content into one turn with several blocks.

That makes transcripts easier to audit. It also matters for tool use, where the turn after an assistant tool_use must be a single user turn that starts with the matching tool_result blocks.
fd9284789f:
A message's content is either a plain string, which is shorthand for one text block, or a list of typed blocks. The list is how one turn mixes instructions, documents, images, tool calls, tool results and reasoning.

Treat it as a polymorphic list with a type discriminator. It's the same pattern as a Jackson @JsonTypeInfo hierarchy, or a sealed interface with records in modern Java. The SDKs model it exactly that way. In Python each block is a typed object with a .type attribute. In Java it's a ContentBlock union with accessors such as text() returning an Optional.
fb37e3096d:
The rule that follows from a polymorphic list is the rule you already apply to any discriminated union: dispatch on the type, never on the position.

Code that reads resp.content[0].text works in the demo. It fails in production the first time the response starts with something else: a thinking block (the default on the newest models, where thinking is adaptive and can't always be turned off), a tool_use block, or no text at all. Example 03_content_blocks.py shows the AttributeError and the fix.

The same rule applies when you store and resend an assistant turn. Keep every block, in order, unmodified. If you filter a response down to its text before appending it to history, you drop the tool_use blocks that the next turn's tool_results refer to. You also drop thinking blocks whose signatures the API checks.
9477767e79:
Every field earns its place.

  • id identifies the message. The separate request-id HTTP header (also exposed as message._request_id in the Python SDK) identifies the HTTP request, and it's what Anthropic support asks for. Log both.
  • model echoes the model that served the call. During an incident review, it's how you prove which model produced a disputed answer. It's also how you notice that an alias moved.
  • content is a list of blocks (section 06).
  • stop_reason is the control signal (section 08). stop_sequence names the custom stop string that fired, or is null.
  • When the stop reason is refusal, a stop_details object identifies the policy category. It is null for every other stop reason.
2bdabd8f52:
usage is your billing and capacity record, and it deserves more attention than it usually gets. input_tokens counts only the uncached input after the last cache breakpoint. Cache writes are reported in cache_creation_input_tokens, and cache reads in cache_read_input_tokens. The total input the model actually processed is the sum of all three.

A dashboard that plots only input_tokens will show a 200,000-token contract review as a 60-token request on the second call. Your cost model will be wrong by orders of magnitude (example 04_usage_accounting.py).

output_tokens includes thinking tokens when thinking is on. Newer responses break those out in usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens (check the docs for which models report it).
e30253e57e:
Two different budgets read this record. Billing charges each of the four counters at its own rate (chapter 15 has the pricing model).

Rate limiting counts input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens toward your input-tokens-per-minute limit. For most current models it does not count cache_read_input_tokens. That's why caching a large shared prefix raises effective throughput as well as cutting cost (section 15).
651226db31:
stop_reason tells you why generation ended. It is the only reliable signal for what your code does next.

A response is an HTTP 200 whether the model finished, ran out of room, wants a tool, paused a server-side loop, or declined. If your code treats every 200 as "here is the answer", four of the seven outcomes become silent bugs. The docs list seven values. Learn them as a table, and then as a dispatch function.
e8aa184726:
Three of these deserve more than a table row.

max_tokens is the most common integration bug in the guide's whole domain. Picture a classifier asked for JSON with a cap of 100 tokens. It works for months. Then a long ticket produces a longer summary field, and the output stops mid-string. Either json.loads throws in a place nobody expected, or, worse, a lenient parser "repairs" it into an object with a missing field.

The model did nothing wrong; your cap did. Example 06_max_tokens_broken_vs_fixed.py shows the crash and the fix. Check the stop reason first, retry once with a larger cap, and fail loudly if it's still truncated.
be0d9bd147: refusal is a normal 200, not an exception, so a generic error handler never sees it. The docs suggest that another Claude model can often serve a refused request, since usage restrictions differ between models. Log it with stop_details. Never retry the identical request on the identical model in a loop.
650951b655:
The empty end_turn is a documented trap. Claude sometimes returns an almost empty response with stop_reason: "end_turn".

The usual cause is adding a text block right after tool_result blocks in the user turn. The model learns to expect user text after tool results, and ends its turn. Another cause is sending Claude's completed answer back without adding anything.

The fix is structural: send tool results with no extra text. If it persists, add a continuation instruction in a new user message, rather than resending the empty response.
37401466a3:
Why not detect completion from the text, for example "the JSON parses" or "the sentence ends with a full stop"? Because both can be true of truncated output. A list of five items truncated after item three is still valid prose. A JSON array cut exactly after a closing brace parses fine, with two objects missing.

The stop reason is the only signal that comes from the generator itself. Chapter 02 applies the same principle to the agent loop: decide what to do next from stop_reason, never by reading the assistant's words for hints such as "I'm done".
ba3f9c2fd9: Structured outputs and strict tool schemas (chapters 18 and 21) guarantee the shape of what the model emits. They can't make a 400-token object fit in a 100-token cap. Even with a schema, check for max_tokens before you trust the result.
16eff11d75: The server forgets everything, so a multi-turn chat is just your code appending to a list and sending the list. The rules are few, and the exam tests them through broken examples:
0e9a08cf92: Append the whole assistant turn. Store every content block of the response, in order and unmodified, not just the text. Dropping tool_use blocks leaves the next turn's tool_results dangling (a 400). Editing thinking blocks breaks their signatures (a 400).
aec3440cb9: Persist outside the process. A pod restart, a deploy, or a load balancer sending turn 4 to a different instance must not lose the conversation. Use Redis, a database row keyed by conversation id, or whatever your platform uses for session state.
cec64bbb24: Decide what the model sees before it overflows. The API won't trim for you unless you turn on a context-management feature explicitly. Trimming, summarising and pinning facts are your job (chapter 03 and objective 6.1).
eefb855033:
The broken version of this function is short and common. It sends only [{"role": "user", "content": user_text}] on each call. It passes a single-turn demo, and fails the first time a customer says "and what about the other line?". Example 07_stateless_multiturn.py runs both.

A subtler variant keeps history in an instance field of a Spring @Service. That bean is a singleton, so every customer shares one transcript. Store state per conversation id, outside the bean.
8db01c6743:
Crude trimming from the front has its own failure. It drops the customer's account number and the original complaint, which are often the facts you need most. The trimming loop above also has to skip forward to a user turn. And in a tool-using conversation, it must never separate a tool_use turn from its tool_result turn.

Better strategies are chapter 03 material: a pinned case-facts block, summarising older turns, pruning bulky tool output first, server-side compaction. The mechanical point here is simpler. Whatever you send is all the model knows.
be3d64ed52:
If the last message in messages is an assistant turn, models that support it continue from that text instead of starting a fresh turn. This is called prefill. It works because the model is a next-token predictor. You've written the first tokens of its answer, so it predicts what follows.

It was used for three things:

  • forcing a format, such as prefilling { to get JSON, or <analysis> to get a tagged section;
  • skipping a chatty preamble;
  • keeping a persona stable in long role-play.

The docs' example pairs it with max_tokens: 1 to get a single multiple-choice letter. The prefill is "The answer is (", and the model emits one token.
c6365558f2:
Four facts about prefill matter for the exam.

  1. The response doesn't include the prefilled text, so you must prepend it yourself. Forgetting is a classic off-by-one-character bug.
  2. Prefill is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models: a trailing assistant turn returns a 400. That covers claude-opus-5-5 and claude-sonnet-5-5.
  3. You can't prefill while thinking is on, on any model.
  4. The documented replacements are structured outputs where supported and system prompt instructions otherwise, plus a tool with an input_schema when you want typed arguments (chapters 18 and 21).
6983a9f042:
Why did Anthropic remove a feature that worked? Prefill lets the client write tokens that the model then treats as its own commitments. That bypasses the model's own planning, including thinking, which must come first in the turn. It's also a known jailbreak vector: prefill "Sure, here is how to..." and the model continues in that voice.

Declared constraints such as a JSON schema give the same format guarantee, without handing the client the model's pen.
659d7b1677:
One legitimate use of an assistant-final message on older models survives in practice: continuing a truncated answer. When a long report stops with max_tokens, you can resend the partial text as the final assistant turn, and the model carries on. On models that reject prefill, keep the partial assistant turn in history and add a user turn asking it to continue from where it stopped. Example 15_continue_after_max_tokens.py implements both paths.

For very long outputs, streaming (chapter 06) or the Batch API (chapter 07) is usually a better answer than chained continuations.
bd7c5591ae: Some options offer "prefill the assistant turn with {" as the way to guarantee schema-valid JSON on a current model. That's wrong twice. It's a 400 on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5. And even where it works, it guarantees only the first character. Structured outputs, or a tool with an input schema, is the stronger answer.
8fc4fb3f93: Tool implementation, descriptions, dispatch, approval patterns and tool-set design belong to chapter 21. This section covers only what the Messages API itself requires. The turn shape is pure protocol, and most tool-related 400s are protocol errors.
39e2311007:
A request declares tools in a top-level tools array. Each has a name, a description and an input_schema (JSON Schema). tool_choice controls selection:

  • {"type": "auto"}: the default; the model decides.
  • {"type": "any"}: the model must call some tool.
  • {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}: the model must call that one.
  • {"type": "none"}.

Forced choices interact with thinking. With manual thinking, only auto and none work. The docs state that Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 reject forced tool use on every request, and recommend auto with strict tool use or structured outputs instead. Check the docs for your model; chapter 21 has the design consequences.
10d38fe516:
When the model decides to call a tool, the response has stop_reason: "tool_use" and one or more tool_use blocks, possibly after some text. Several blocks in one response are parallel tool calls.

Your next request must contain the assistant turn exactly as received. After it comes a user turn whose content starts with one tool_result for every tool_use id. Missing any id is a 400. Putting a text block before the results is a 400. Putting text after them invites the empty end_turn described in section 08.

Mark a failed call with is_error: true. Then the model knows the content is an error message, not data, and can recover.
86bfd1bcab:
Two related stop reasons complete the picture. Server tools (tools Anthropic runs, such as web search) execute inside the API call. Their calls and results appear as server-tool blocks in the response. If the server-side loop hits its iteration limit, the response stops with pause_turn. You resume by sending the assistant content back unchanged, with the same tools.

Your own tools never produce pause_turn; they produce tool_use. Example 09_tool_turn_shape.py sends the broken and fixed result turns through the strict fake.
e8e34476b8: What extended and adaptive thinking are, when they help, and how effort trades quality for latency is chapter 13 material. Here we need only the wire format. It changed across model generations, and a request written for one generation is a 400 on another.
228e39f399:
Four mechanics bite in practice.

max_tokens includes thinking. A 16,000 cap with heavy thinking can leave little room for the answer. A max_tokens stop with only a thinking block is a real outcome.

Thinking blocks must be round-tripped. Within a tool-use turn, every thinking and redacted_thinking block must go back complete and unmodified alongside its tool_use. Edited blocks are a 400. And code that filters on block.type == "thinking" silently drops redacted_thinking and breaks the protocol.

What you see is not all you pay for. On the newest models the default display is "omitted". Thinking blocks arrive with an empty thinking field and an opaque signature, and you are still billed for the thinking tokens. display: "summarized" returns a summary instead.

Incompatibilities. There's no prefill with thinking. Forced tool_choice is restricted, as in section 11. On older models, temperature and top_k are incompatible with thinking, and top_p is limited to 0.95 to 1. Changing the thinking configuration between turns also invalidates prompt-cache breakpoints (chapter 15).

Example 10_thinking_params.py runs seven configurations against the strict fake.
2a4b98fcfd: When a request fails, the API returns a non-2xx status and a JSON body with a fixed shape. It has a top-level type: "error", an error object with its own type and message, and a request_id that matches the request-id header. The docs warn that new error types may be added over time. So code that switches on error.type needs a default branch.
9679132925: For each status, the one decision you must make is whether a retry can help. The principle is the one you already apply to any distributed system. Retry conditions that are transient and on the server's side. Never retry a request that is wrong, because it will be wrong again. The table lists every status the errors page documents.
93e486f73c:
Three failure classes don't appear in that table, and they catch teams out.

Connection failures and client timeouts produce no HTTP status at all. The SDKs raise APIConnectionError or APITimeoutError (Python) and AnthropicIoException (Java). They are retryable.

Errors inside a stream arrive after the API has already returned a 200 and started sending events. Ordinary status-code handling never sees them. Chapter 06 covers the error event and the Java SseException.

And a 200 can still be a functional failure. max_tokens, model_context_window_exceeded and refusal are successful HTTP responses that your code must treat as failures of the task.
cbae0e7e86:
Two operational details complete the picture.

The SDKs refuse to send a non-streaming request whose max_tokens means it's expected to run longer than about ten minutes. The docs recommend streaming or the Batch API for anything long, because networks drop idle connections.

And watch two spend errors. The 400 for an organisation spend limit looks like a code problem. The 429 for a tier spend cap looks like a capacity problem. They're neither. Alert a human rather than retrying or redeploying.
73d89e8fba:
The SDKs already retry. By default the Python and Java SDKs retry twice (three attempts in total) with short exponential backoff. They do this on connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx responses, and they honour retry-after when it's present. The default request timeout is ten minutes.

For many services those defaults are fine. The right move is to tune max_retries and timeout rather than write your own loop. You write your own policy when you need something the SDK doesn't do: log each attempt with the request id, switch to a fallback model after repeated 529s, give up early because a user is waiting, or refuse to retry a 429 that has no retry-after.
17c5f103db:
A good policy has five properties.

  • It classifies: it retries only the green box in FIG 9.
  • It honours retry-after. The server knows when capacity returns, and retries sent earlier simply fail.
  • It uses exponential backoff with jitter. A thousand clients that all wait exactly 1, 2, 4 seconds retry in synchronised waves and keep the service overloaded. Full jitter (a random delay between zero and the exponential ceiling) spreads them out.
  • It is capped in attempts and total time. A user-facing request that retries for three minutes has already failed.
  • And it lives in exactly one layer.
6106b329e8:
The single-layer rule is the one most often broken in enterprise stacks, and it's pure arithmetic. The SDK retries twice. A developer adds an application loop that retries twice. The platform team wraps outbound HTTP in a Resilience4j retry that also retries twice. Each layer multiplies: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 attempts per user request.

During a 529 incident with 200 concurrent users, that's 5,400 requests pointed at an API that is already overloaded. Your own rate limit then turns the next ten minutes into 429s.

Pick one layer to own retries, and set the others to zero (max_retries=0 on the client if your code owns it). Example 16_retry_stacking.py prints the table. 12_retry_backoff.py runs the classified policy against scripted 429, 529 and 400 responses.
6f1d2b1a0f: Retries also need idempotency thinking. A Messages call has no side effects on Anthropic's side, so resending it is safe. But suppose your agent's tool executed a refund before the next model call failed. Retrying the whole turn from the start would execute it again. Retry the model call, not the business transaction. Chapter 21 covers idempotency keys for tools.
20855883fe: Rate limits on the Messages API are set per organisation, per usage tier and per model class. So Sonnet and Haiku traffic draw on separate allowances. Each model class has three dimensions: requests per minute (RPM), input tokens per minute (ITPM) and output tokens per minute (OTPM). Each usage tier also has a monthly spend cap. The numbers change by tier and over time. Read them in the console and the docs rather than memorising them.
e0ebb13f8e:
Enforcement uses a token bucket. Capacity refills continuously up to your maximum, rather than resetting at the top of each minute. Two consequences follow. A burst can be rejected even when your per-minute average is under the limit; the docs note that a 60 RPM limit may be enforced as one request per second. And there is no "wait for the new minute" trick, because capacity returns gradually.

Separately, an acceleration limit can return 429s when an organisation's usage rises sharply, even below the per-minute limits. The documented remedy is to ramp traffic up gradually and keep usage patterns steady. A Black-Friday launch that goes from zero to full load in one second is exactly the case it catches.
eee3548e7d:
Two counting rules are worth knowing exactly, because intuition gets both wrong.

Cache reads do not count toward ITPM for most current models. Only input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens do. A 200,000-token cached policy document with a 50-token question costs 50 tokens of ITPM on a cache hit.

OTPM counts tokens actually generated, in real time. max_tokens doesn't factor in, so a generous cap carries no rate-limit penalty. (It still affects how long a non-streaming request may take.)
a422ea9b97: Read those headers on every response. The Python SDK exposes them through client.messages.with_raw_response.create(...), and Java through withRawResponse(). Use them to adapt before you hit a 429: halve concurrency when a remaining value falls below a quarter of its limit, and restore it when the bucket refills. Example 14_rate_limit_headers.py does exactly that. It shows that output tokens, not requests, were the binding limit for its workload.
b5189b2674:
The better fix is usually not to hit the limit at all. A client-side token bucket in front of the API (example 13_token_bucket.py; in Java, Bucket4j or a Resilience4j RateLimiter) smooths a burst into a steady flow that stays under ITPM.

Beyond that, the levers are architectural:

  • cache the shared prefix, so most input is cache reads;
  • move latency-tolerant work to the Batch API, which has its own limits and half the price (chapter 07);
  • spread traffic across model classes where quality allows, since each has its own allowance;
  • request a higher tier when the steady-state need is real.
35afa6c227:
The official SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, C#, Ruby, PHP and others) are typed wrappers over the same REST endpoint. Chapter 14 shows the raw HTTP they generate. Knowing what they add tells you what you'd have to build yourself with a plain HTTP client:

  • typed request and response models;
  • API key loading from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and the version header;
  • automatic retries with backoff, and timeouts;
  • typed exceptions per status;
  • access to the request id and raw headers;
  • streaming helpers that accumulate events into a final message;
  • pagination for list endpoints, and helpers such as token counting.
1f905e06e4: The Python exception classes map one-to-one onto statuses: BadRequestError (400), AuthenticationError (401), PermissionDeniedError (403), NotFoundError (404), ConflictError (409), UnprocessableEntityError (422), RateLimitError (429) and InternalServerError (5xx). All are subclasses of APIStatusError, which is itself an APIError. APIConnectionError covers failures with no response. Catch the most specific classes first.
4996dbe297:
The Java SDK (com.anthropic:anthropic-java; the docs showed version 2.70.0 at the time of writing, Java 8 or later) follows builder conventions you already know.

Create one client per application, because each client owns connection and thread pools. In Spring that means a singleton bean. AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv() reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; system properties such as anthropic.apiKey take precedence. Retries default to two and the timeout to ten minutes, and both are set on the builder. client.async() or AnthropicOkHttpClientAsync returns CompletableFutures.
4fba06e519:
The Java exceptions follow the same shape:

  • AnthropicServiceException for HTTP errors, with subclasses BadRequestException, UnauthorizedException, PermissionDeniedException, NotFoundException, UnprocessableEntityException, RateLimitException, InternalServerException and UnexpectedStatusCodeException;
  • AnthropicIoException for network failures;
  • SseException for errors mid-stream.

All of them sit under AnthropicException.

Model constants such as Model.CLAUDE_OPUS_5_5 exist alongside a String overload. The stop-reason comparison above uses toString() to stay independent of the exact enum constant names, which you should confirm in the Javadocs. The system(...) builder method wasn't shown on the SDK page we checked, so confirm it in the Javadocs as well.
d773ece731:
Every rule in this chapter can be tested without a network call. It should be, because these are exactly the bugs that slip through a happy-path demo.

The companion's StrictFakeClient extends the shared fake from chapter 01 with three things:

  • scripted replies with an explicit stop_reason;
  • scripted HTTP errors with headers;
  • request validation that rejects what the real API rejects: system role first, prefill or non-default sampling on new models, unanswered tool calls, invalid thinking budgets.

In Java the same idea is a hand-written fake of a small ClaudeGateway interface. Or use WireMock, stubbing /v1/messages with recorded JSON bodies and 429/529 responses.
29cb1359e7:
Be clear about what these tests prove: your code handles every outcome the protocol can produce. They prove nothing about answer quality. That needs evaluation against the real model (chapter 16 on debugging, and the evaluation chapters).

They also encode today's rules. When a model upgrade changes a rule, the fake must change with it. That's a useful forcing function: the upgrade checklist (chapter 10) should include "update the strict fake and rerun".
6f3628dfe7: CCDV-F items on API mechanics give a symptom and four fixes. The wrong options are usually model-quality fixes for protocol bugs, or retry fixes for non-retryable errors. Work each one before reading the reasoning.
1f8afd95f7: Failures concentrated on long inputs, with a parse error, are the signature of truncation. The summary grew and the output hit the cap, and the response says so in stop_reason. A and C treat a protocol limit as a model behaviour problem; no model can exceed your cap. D is worst. It turns a detectable failure into silently missing fields.
47d2740374: The server keeps no state. Only what is in messages exists for the model. A misdiagnoses: the window isn't the problem when only one turn is sent. C confuses caching (a cost and latency optimisation for a prefix you still send) with memory. D is wrong twice. metadata.user_id is an opaque abuse-detection id that the model doesn't read, and it must never contain personal data.
f15bbfcb74: Stacked layers multiply attempts (3 × 4 × 3 = 36 per request here). That amplifies the overload and burns the organisation's own rate limit. 529 is transient and retryable, so D gives up too early. A and C add load to an overloaded service. One owning layer with backoff and jitter, plus a degradation path, is the standard answer.
9eabaaa728: Every tool_use id must be answered in the next user turn, results first. A failed tool is still answered, flagged with is_error so the model can recover. A changes nothing relevant. B breaks the pairing by dropping the assistant turn. D retries a 400, which fails identically.
f89413f7d4:
On the newest models, both non-default sampling parameters and assistant prefill are rejected with 400. The documented replacements are structured outputs or instructions. C confuses the API contract version with model behaviour. D still sends a non-default temperature and the prefill. A is unnecessary.

The lesson is objective 5.3's "breaking changes across releases". A model ID is not a drop-in config value. Pin it, read the migration notes, and run evals before switching.
af37edf7e0: Done when: you can recite the seven stop reasons and their handlers. You can sort any status code into fix, page or retry within five seconds. You can explain why the API is stateless and what that costs. And you can say why prefill and temperature: 0 break on the newest models.
